one_liner: Header-only, policy-based type erasure whose zoo::Function holds move-only callables inline, beating std::function plus a shared_ptr workaround.
what_it_does: zoo is a header-only C++17 component library; its type-erasure core is AnyContainer, configured by a Policy that names the inline buffer (for example void*[2]) and the operations the erased type must support (Destroy, Move, Copy, RTTI, a call signature). zoo::Function<AnyContainer<...>, R(Args...)> layers a std::function-like call operator, operator bool and nullptr comparison on top, and with a Move-only policy it accepts move-only captures that std::function rejects. The interface is close to std::function but the type is spelled through policies; the short alias zoo::function is a different, copyable AnyCallable<Any, Sig> and is not what was benchmarked.
how_it_is_fast: The callable is stored in a small buffer whose size and alignment are a template parameter, so the caller can match or exceed std::function's inline capacity; targets that are not nothrow-move-constructible, too large or misaligned fall back to a single heap allocation (BuilderDecider in VTablePolicy.h). Each policy builds one static, constexpr vtable of only the requested operations, and zoo::Function keeps the invoker pointer in the object, so a call is one indirect jump with no empty-check branch (the empty state holds a throwing executor). The headline 3x comes from holding a unique_ptr capture inline with one allocation, where std::function needs make_shared plus its own heap block (3 allocations under libstdc++, 2 under libc++).
when_to_use: Job queues, thread-pool enqueue paths or callbacks that must own move-only state (unique_ptr, file handles) and today wrap it in shared_ptr to satisfy std::function's copyability.
Pre-C++23 toolchains without std::move_only_function, or libc++ builds where you want a move-only function with a small inline buffer and zoo's smaller object (40 vs 48 bytes in the tt-metal run).
Code that wants to choose inline capacity per type (void*[N]) and pay only for the operations it needs (no Copy entry for move-only, RTTI only if wanted).

Codebases that want smaller object code and faster builds than std::function: in the tt-metal measurement zoo had the smallest .text in all three configurations and compiled 300 instantiations in 2.88 s against 7.46 s under libc++.
when_not_to_use: Copyable callables with small captures where you already use std::function: the inline construct-invoke-destroy gain is about 0.3 ns (2.3 vs 2.6 ns), and small-capture move construction under libstdc++ was slower (3.74 vs 2.34 ns on gcc-12, 6.91 vs 2.34 ns on clang-20).
Builds with -fno-rtti: typeid in VTablePolicy.h and FunctionPolicy.h breaks compilation even without the RTTI policy (per the tt-metal evaluation).
When you can use C++23 std::move_only_function, the fair baseline, which was never measured against zoo.

Projects that need tagged releases or a stable API: zoo has no tags or releases, recent commits are documentation, and the README calls the released CppCon 2022 code a complete implementation that may not be production-ready.
Code that assigns callables whose construction can throw and must stay exception-safe (see gotchas).

integration.dependencies: none for the headers (Catch2 submodule only for tests)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; CI builds tests with g++-9, clang-17 and MSVC (MSVC failures do not block changes); the tt-metal evaluation used g++-12 and clang++-20 in C++20 mode
integration.platforms: any (portable C++17); no SIMD or OS requirements in the type-erasure headers
integration.thread_safety: not documented; it is a value type like std::function (no internal synchronisation)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the call syntax, operator bool and nullptr comparisons match std::function, but the type must be spelled as zoo::Function<zoo::AnyContainer<zoo::Policy<void*[N], zoo::Destroy, zoo::Move, zoo::RTTI>>, Sig> (add Copy for copyability), and target()/target_type() exist only on the separate zoo::function alias; tt-metal needed a wrapper of about 45 lines for its own checks.

gotchas: Assigning a new callable destroys the old target first and then constructs the new one in place (AnyContainerBase::emplace_impl); if that construction throws (bad_alloc on the heap path or a throwing capture constructor) the object is left with a vtable for a value that was never built, so later destruction is undefined. std::function's assignment gives the strong guarantee. Source reading, not tested.

A moved-from zoo::Function stays engaged: the defaulted move keeps the executor and, on the heap path, nulls only the target pointer, so operator bool still returns true and calling it invokes a moved-from or null target, where libstdc++'s std::function is left empty and throws bad_function_call. Source reading, not tested.

The tt-metal README says zoo's noexcept move entry accepts throwing-move targets and would terminate; the pinned VTablePolicy.h (identical to master) routes any type that is not nothrow-move-constructible to the heap (ByReference), whose move only steals the pointer, so that terminate path does not appear in the source.
The repo's own benchmark (benchmark/catch2Functions.cpp) only stores plain function pointers and, unless built with USE_FOLLY, its 'folly' column is a std::function alias; it publishes no numbers.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick zoo over stdext::inplace_function, SmallFunction or Delegate when the callable must own move-only state and you still want a heap fallback for large captures; those siblings were measured only on copyable or inline targets. woid and sy_callback target call speed of copyable callables; zoo's measured win is allocation count on the move-only path, plus smaller code and faster compiles than std::function.
verified_claims_summary: In tenstorrent's tt-metal harness (Google Benchmark 1.9.1, Release build, median of 5 repetitions, 32-thread x86-64 host with 48 KiB L1d and 1.25 MiB L2 per core, CPU model not named) zoo::Function with a void*[N] buffer pinned to std::function's inline size ran a unique_ptr-capture construct/invoke/destroy in 12.7-14.0 ns against 42.7-45.6 ns for std::function holding a shared_ptr wrapper (about 3.1-3.6x) on gcc-12/libstdc++, clang-20/libstdc++ and clang-20/libc++, and an enqueue-1024-then-drain std::deque loop 1.09-1.24x faster. Other rows are mixed: inline construct-invoke-destroy is about 1.13x faster, while small-capture move construction under libstdc++ and large-capture move assignment under libc++ are slower than std::function.
status_note: MIT-licensed and header-only, so easy to vendor, but untagged (pin by SHA; tt-metal pinned master HEAD 7fb5eed of 2026-04-15), the ten latest commits are documentation edits, and 18 pull requests and 10 issues are open.
